core: The interest rate as the price of borrowing money and the reward for saving, expressed as a percent per year
Nominal vs real interest rates and the Fisher relationship (real interest rate approximately equals the nominal rate minus expected inflation)
How market interest rates are set in the market for loanable funds: saving supplies funds, borrowing demands them, and the equilibrium rate clears the market
How a central bank influences short-term interest rates by setting a target for the policy (federal funds) rate
Why different loans carry different rates: default risk, term/maturity, inflation expectations, and liquidity
Present value / discounting: a dollar received later is worth less than a dollar now, and higher interest rates lower present value
supporting: The equilibrium interest rate as the price where quantity of funds demanded equals quantity supplied
That an unexpected rise in inflation transfers value from lenders to borrowers when the loan rate is fixed
That a change in the policy rate is reflected in other short-term borrowing costs and influences longer-term rates

claims.claim: The interest rate is the price paid to borrow money and the reward earned for saving or lending it, stated as a percent of the principal per year; in a financial market it is the price that brings the quantity of funds supplied and demanded into balance.

Savers (those who make financial investments) are on the supply side of the financial market and borrowers are on the demand side; the equilibrium interest rate is where quantity of funds demanded equals quantity supplied, and rates above or below equilibrium create surpluses or shortages that push the rate back.

The nominal interest rate is the stated percentage; the real interest rate adjusts for inflation and approximately equals the nominal rate minus inflation, so with 4 percent nominal interest and 5 percent inflation the real return is about negative 1 percent.

When a loan's interest rate is fixed, an unexpected rise in inflation penalizes lenders (repaid in dollars worth less) and benefits borrowers (repay in cheaper dollars), which is why expected inflation is built into nominal rates.

Suppliers of financial capital weigh the rate of return against the risk involved, so lenders demand a higher interest rate to bear higher default risk; differences in risk are a central reason different borrowers pay different rates.

The Federal Reserve conducts monetary policy chiefly by changing its target for the federal funds rate, and a change in that rate is rapidly reflected in the short-term interest rates banks and other lenders charge households and businesses and also influences longer-term rates; since 2008 the target is stated as a 25-basis-point range. Congress directs the Fed to promote maximum employment, stable prices, and moderate long-term interest rates.

Present discounted value equals a future amount divided by (1 + interest rate) raised to the number of years; at a 10 percent interest rate a 110 dollar payment one year from now has a present value of 100 dollars, because 100 dollars today grows to 110 dollars in a year.

Because present value divides by (1 + interest rate) raised to the term, a higher interest rate lowers present value: a two-year bond paying 240 dollars then 3,240 dollars is worth 3,000 dollars when discounted at 8 percent but only about 2,845.80 dollars when discounted at 11 percent.
A dollar received in the future is worth less than a dollar today, so present value is the indispensable tool for comparing costs and benefits that arrive at different times.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Exact vs approximate real interest rate
positions: The teaching approximation: real rate = nominal rate minus (expected) inflation
The exact Fisher identity: 1 + real = (1 + nominal) / (1 + inflation), which for 6 percent nominal and 4 percent inflation gives 1.923 percent rather than the 2 percent approximation
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the subtraction approximation (standard at the introductory level and used by OpenStax) and notes it is an approximation, giving the verified exact figure so no precision is misstated.
